claims.text: Oxidation resistance and material integrity in high-temperature multiprincipal-element alloys are primarily governed by the ability to form and maintain a continuous, adherent oxide scale enriched in Cr and Al.
The baseline alloy contains moderate levels of Cr and Al along with several other principal elements.
Cr and Al are oxidation-promoting elements in the proposed alloy system.
Some of the other alloying elements being reduced do not contribute to oxide-scale formation.
Increasing Cr and Al will promote formation of a continuous protective layer dominated by Cr2O3 and Al2O3.
The Cr2O3- and Al2O3-dominated layer will adhere well to the substrate.
Higher Cr and Al concentrations promote rapid formation of a stable and continuous oxide film.
The stable, continuous oxide film acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress.
Reduced oxygen diffusion slows oxide-scale growth.
Reduced oxygen diffusion slows internal oxidation.
Slower scale growth and internal oxidation preserve the alloy's microstructural integrity.
The Cr- and Al-enhanced alloy will have a lower oxidation rate than the baseline alloy.
The Cr- and Al-enhanced alloy will form a thinner oxide scale than the baseline alloy.
The Cr- and Al-enhanced alloy will form a more adherent oxide scale than the baseline alloy.
The Cr- and Al-enhanced alloy will retain mechanical integrity better than the baseline alloy.
The proposed governing behavior should hold in oxidizing environments at approximately 900–1100°C for exposures of 100–500 hours.
At significantly higher temperatures, different degradation mechanisms may dominate.
In non-oxidizing environments, different degradation mechanisms may dominate.
Composition changes that increase Cr and Al may induce phase instabilities that alter oxidation behavior.
